overview.text: A prion is an infectious, abnormally folded form of the body’s prion protein (PrP). Its unusual feature is that the abnormal shape can bind to normally folded PrP and promote its conversion into more misfolded protein. As this protein accumulates in the brain, it can form clumps and damage or destroy neurons, causing serious neurodegenerative disease. Prion diseases affect humans and other animals: examples include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in people and bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE, or “mad cow disease”) in cattle. They can arise spontaneously, be associated with inherited changes in the PRNP gene, or result from exposure to prions. Thus, the term describes an unusual infectious protein mechanism, not a claim that every case spreads between people.

key_facts.text: The PRNP gene carries instructions for making the body’s prion protein; its normal function is not fully understood.
Abnormally folded PrP can bind to normal PrP and promote its conversion, although the process is not fully understood.
Misfolded PrP can accumulate in the brain, forming clumps that damage or destroy neurons.
Prion diseases may be sporadic, associated with inherited gene changes, or acquired after exposure to prions.
Examples include CJD in people and BSE in cattle; prion diseases also affect other animals.
